newsitem.title: BELGIUM: Euro seen chipping away at dollar's global reach.
newsitem.headline: Euro seen chipping away at dollar's global reach.

text.p: A single European currency will gradually erode the dollar's dominance on global markets and transform the world's monetary regime into a bi-polar system, the EU is expected to say on Wednesday.

In its first attempt to assess the broader implications of economic and monetary union (EMU), the European Commission is seen taking a cautious yet upbeat stance on the euro's ability to rival the dollar.

While the dollar's use as a reserve currency has declined in recent years -- 63 percent of official reserves were held in dollars compared with 76 percent in 1973 -- it is still by far the most dominant currency traded on foreign exchange markets.
The dollar is involved in 83 percent of global foreign exchange transactions, with a strong role in swaps and futures markets in Asia.

Interest in the international dimension of the single currency, the euro, has grown in recent weeks, with monetary officials throughout the industrialised world beginning to ponder its broader ramifications.

At a recent conference in Washington, there was a consensus among international officials that the euro's attractiveness would likely be determined by the economic policy stance in Europe and the success of a European Central Bank (ECB) in achieving low inflation.

Among the key questions considered at the IMF-sponsored meeting were the prospects for international economic policy coordination -- what EMU would mean for coordination within the Group of Seven industrialised nations, for example.

The Commission paper is likely to touch on this issue as well, suggesting the possiblity of a high level economic representative from the euro area who along with the president of the ECB would help coordinate policy inside the G7.

Where the euro is seen having an immediate advantage is as an anchor currency for Europe, extending to the countries of eastern and central Europe, the Mediterranean and several African Sub-Saharan countries.
Another important factor in the euro's early success will be the development of broad and deep European bond and equity markets.
If all EU countries eventually join EMU, the resulting bond market would become the largest in the world, prompting significant portfolio shifts among global investors.

New debt issued by goverments in the EMU area will be denominated in the euro. While Belgium and France have said they would also redenominate their outstanding debt, there is still doubt over whether countries like Germany will follow.

Another potential advantage will be in trade invoicing. Although the United States accounts for only 12 percent of world trade, roughly 48 percent is invoiced in dollars. The situation could be radically altered with the emergence of the euro since the EU accounts for about 38 percent of world exports and imports.
Where the euro will have a tough time gaining an edge on the dollar, however, is in Asia and some of the emerging markets of Latin and South America. Here, the greenback remains king.

Recent figures show that close to 48 percent of Japanese exports and 75 percent of imports are priced in dollars. The U.S. currency's strong role in the region extends to the financial centres of Singapore and Hong Kong.
